en: Therīgāthā 14.1: The Chapter of Thirty (Tiṁsanipāta),
The Verse of the Elder Nun Subhājīvakambavanikā.
As the beautiful nun was going toward the delightful Jīvakambavana grove,
a rogue blocked her way.
Subhā said to him:
"What offense have I committed against you,
that you stand there obstructing me?"
For it is not fitting, friend, for one who has gone forth to touch a man;
this is a heavy matter in the teaching of my Teacher.
Why do you stand obstructing me, when there is this training taught by the Sugata— a state of utter purity, free from blemish?
One with a turbid mind [approaches] one who is clear,
one full of passion [approaches] one free from passion and blemishless,
[and one approaches] one whose mind is liberated in every respect.
"Why do you stand there obstructing me?
You are young and blameless;
what will renunciation do for you?"
Set aside your saffron robe;
come, let us enjoy ourselves in this forest in full bloom.
Sweet scents waft from every direction.
The trees have burst forth with pollen;
this first springtime is a pleasant season.
Come, let us delight in the forest in full bloom.
And the trees with flowering crests,
stirred by the wind, seem as if they are roaring;
what delight will there be for you?
If you alone shall enter the forest,
which is frequented by herds of wild beasts and agitated by intoxicated elephants and their female mates;
"Without a companion you wish to go,
to the desolate and terrifying great forest,
O lady clad in refined gold."
You move like a celestial nymph, a creeper of the mind;
you shine with garments as fine as delicate Kāsī cloth, O peerless one.
I would be subject to your will,
if we were to dwell together in the forest;
for there is nothing dearer to me than you.
O Kinnarī with eyes like a mandala,
if you will follow my word,
come and live happily at home.
Dwelling in a pleasant, cool residence,
let women perform service for you;
wear garments of fine Kāsī cloth.
And put on this garland and ointment;
I shall provide you with much gold, gems, and pearls,
and various kinds of ornaments.
Ascend this beautiful, costly bed, newly spread with a well-washed royal coverlet and stuffed with fine wool and cotton.
It was scented with the essence of sandalwood ornaments,
like a blue lotus risen from the water,
frequented by non-human beings.
"In this way, you, though practicing the holy life,
will grow old among your own limbs.
"What do you consider to be the essence here?"
In this body, which is full of putrefaction, increases the cemetery, and is subject to dissolution—
seeing what is it that you look on with such dejection?
“Like two blue lotuses,
like two kinnarīs in the midst of the mountains—
having beheld your eyes, my own eyes [have become so]...”
Their delight in sensual pleasures increases all the more.
Your faces are like the tips of blue lotuses,
stainless and resembling refined gold.
Having beheld your eyes,
my desire for sensual pleasures increases all the more;
even though you have gone far away, you are still remembered by me.
O you with long lashes and pure vision!
O Kinnarī with eyes like those of a deer, there is indeed nothing dearer to me than your eyes.”
“You wish to cross over with indifference;
you seek to play with the moon;
you wish to leap over Mount Meru.”
You who seek after the Son of the Buddha—
indeed, there is no passion remaining for me anywhere now, even in this world with its devas.
Nor do I know what kind it was,
but now it has been destroyed by the path along with its roots,
cast away like a pit of embers.
Like a poisoned bowl placed over a fire,
I do not see what kind of state it has reached,
now that it has been destroyed along with its roots by the path.
If there should be one who has not reflected,
or one who has not attended upon the Teacher—
tempt such a person as that.
Knowing this, you are distressed.
For when reviling and praising,
and pleasure and pain, are present, I remain established [in equanimity].
Knowing that all conditioned things are impure,
my mind clings to nothing at all.
Such am I, a disciple of the Sugata.
Travelling by means of the vehicle of the Eightfold Path,
with arrows extracted and free from taints,
I delight in having gone to an empty dwelling.
For I have seen well-constructed wooden pegs, complete with cords and stakes.
Bound together, they performed various dances.
When that [loom] was removed— the warp-peg discarded,
the threads loosened, and it dismantled— [they too vanished].
If one were to find nothing when [the body] is cut into pieces,
where in that regard could one fix the mind?
Bodies are just like that for me.
Without those phenomena they do not proceed;
since nothing proceeds without phenomena,
wherein therein should one fix the mind?
Just as one might see a painting on a wall smeared with yellow orpiment,
so too was your perception of that [object] inverted.
Human perception is useless;
it is like an illusion created before one's eyes,
or like a golden tree seen in a dream.
You approach the blind and empty one,
like a puppet in the midst of people;
you are like a worm dwelling within a rotting fruit.
In the middle there are bubbles accompanied by tears;
pustules and boils arise here,
as well as various kinds of eye-diseases, all clustered together.
Having gouged out [the eyes] of that one of beautiful appearance,
she did not yield, her mind being free from attachment:
"Come now, take this eye of yours."
He gave it to that man at once.
And for him, passion ceased at once, and he asked his forgiveness there.
“May you be safe, O practitioner of the holy life;
such a thing shall not happen again.
“Having encountered such a person as this...”
As if embracing a blazing fire,
or as if grasping a venomous snake—
would there indeed be safety? Please forgive us!
Then that nun, having been released from there,
went into the presence of the Excellent Buddha;
she beheld the marks of supreme merit.
"The eye was as it was before. ...
The Elder Nun Subhā Jīvakambavanikā.
The Book of Thirties is concluded.
